screens.title: Network Interfaces and Naming
screens.narratorSegment: A network interface is the hardware or virtual device that connects your system to a network. It’s the boundary where packets enter and leave a host. Common names include lo for loopback, which is used for local-only traffic and testing; traditional eth0 or eth1 for Ethernet devices; and predictable names such as enp0s3 which tie the name to physical bus location. Knowing the name matters because commands and connection profiles target interfaces by name. For example, when adding a temporary IP you will specify the device name; when creating an nmcli profile you bind it to a specific ifname. A common misconception is that interface names are arbitrary and interchangeable — changing or misidentifying the target interface can configure the wrong device and leave your system without network. An example: if your primary interface is enp0s3 but you add a static IP to eth0, nothing will change for the active link. To confirm the active interface, use ip link show and ip addr show. Practice: run ip addr show and identify which interface has the default gateway route in the routing table. Takeaway: always confirm the interface name and link state before making changes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Network Interfaces
Definition

What a network interface is

An interface binds a device to IP addresses, MAC addresses, and link state. It’s the target for ip and NetworkManager commands.

Common names
lo, eth0, enp0s3 and similar predictable names.
Why naming changed
Predictable names reduce confusion across reboots and hardware reordering.
Common mistake
Assuming eth0 exists on modern systems — always confirm with ip link show.
Example
$ ip addr show 2: enp0s3: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 inet 192.168.1.10/24 brd 192.168.1.255 scope global dynamic enp0s3 1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536 inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
Check link state
Use ip link show to see whether interfaces are UP or DOWN before changes.
Key Takeaway
Always verify the target interface name and link state to avoid unintended outages.

screens.title: Using the ip command
screens.narratorSegment: The ip command family is the modern toolkit for inspecting and temporarily manipulating network state. Start by running ip addr show to list interfaces and their addresses; ip link show reveals link state and MAC addresses; ip route show prints the kernel routing table and the default gateway. These three outputs together explain where traffic will flow and whether the link is up. For example, ip route show often contains a line like default via 192.168.1.1 dev enp0s3 which tells you the gateway and the outgoing interface. When you need to test a new address without changing the persistent configuration, you can add a temporary IP with sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.100/24 dev enp0s3 and remove it with ip addr del when done. A frequent misconception is confusing temporary ip changes with persistent configuration. Remember that ip commands affect the running kernel only and will be lost after reboot. Always plan how you will persist changes if they need to survive or revert them safely if experimenting remotely. Try combining ip route get to see which interface the kernel would use toward a specific destination.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › The ip Command
Command Reference

Inspect addresses and links

# show addresses
ip addr show

# show link states
ip link show

# show routing table
ip route show
Temporary IP example
sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.100/24 dev enp0s3
sudo ip link set enp0s3 up
# test
ping -c 4 8.8.8.8
# remove
sudo ip addr del 192.168.1.100/24 dev enp0s3
Explanation
  • ip addr shows assignment and CIDR mask; read the /24 as subnet size.
  • ip route reveals which gateway handles outbound traffic and which device is used.
  • ip route get helps determine what interface the kernel will choose for a given destination.
Key Takeaway

Use ip for immediate, transient changes and to diagnose how the kernel will route traffic.

screens.title: Temporary vs Persistent Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: When you need to test network settings without committing them, use ip to make temporary changes. These are useful for experiments, troubleshooting, or when you need to test a new IP before persisting it. The process is: 1) identify the active interface with ip addr show, 2) bring the interface down if you must, but be careful when remote, 3) add a temporary address with ip addr add, 4) bring the link up, test connectivity, then 5) remove the address with ip addr del. Persistent configuration is handled by a network configuration service, commonly NetworkManager on many distributions. NetworkManager stores profiles and reapplies settings after reboot, so use nmcli connection add or modify to create durable profiles. A common pitfall is assuming ip changes persist — they do not. Another trap is doing link-down operations on a remote server without a safety plan. For safe remote work, schedule an automatic revert or have console access. Example: add a test IP, ping a known server, then delete the address. If it must persist, create an nmcli profile rather than editing /etc/resolv. conf directly when NetworkManager manages the file.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Temporary vs Persistent
Step-by-step

Safe temporary IP test

  1. Identify interface: ip addr show & ip route show.
  2. Add address: sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.200/24 dev <iface>.
  3. Bring link up if needed: sudo ip link set <iface> up.
  4. Test connectivity: ping -c 4 8.8.8.8 and ping -c 4 google.com.
  5. Remove test address: sudo ip addr del 192.168.1.200/24 dev <iface>.
When to persist

If the change must survive reboots, create a NetworkManager connection profile using nmcli instead of using ip for permanence. That way the settings are stored and reapplied by the service.

Example nmcli command
sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name "StaticTest" ifname enp0s3 ip4 192.168.1.50/24 gw4 192.168.1.1
Warning

Bringing an interface down on a remote host can disconnect you. Always plan a rollback or console access.

screens.title: NetworkManager, nmcli and nmtui
screens.narratorSegment: NetworkManager is a background service that centralizes network configuration and makes it easier to manage dynamic and persistent connections. It stores connection profiles you can list with nmcli connection show and the device state with nmcli device status. nmcli is the command-line interface that lets you create, modify, bring up, or bring down profiles. nmtui is a curses-based interactive interface useful on systems without a graphical environment. Use nmcli connection add to create a static profile: specify type ethernet, con-name, ifname, ip4 with CIDR, and gw4 for the gateway. After creating a profile, nmcli connection up will activate it. If you need to change DNS for that profile, use nmcli connection modify "Name" ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4". A misconception is that editing resolv. conf directly is always the right approach. When NetworkManager or systemd-resolved manages the file, manual edits may be overwritten. Prefer to configure DNS through NetworkManager or resolved if they are active. Use nmtui when a guided, keyboard-driven workflow is faster, and use nmcli scripts for repeatable automation. NetworkManager, nmcli and nmtui means networkmanager manages persistent profiles and should be the primary tool for durable configuration on systems where it runs.. In practical terms, high-level network management and how to interact with it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › NetworkManager
Components

nmcli and nmtui

# list devices
nmcli device status

# list connections
nmcli connection show

# create static
sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name "MyStaticNet" ifname enp0s3 ip4 192.168.1.10/24 gw4 192.168.1.1
Best practices
  • When NetworkManager manages the host, prefer nmcli or nmtui to change settings rather than editing files directly.
  • Create named profiles so you can easily bring them up or delete them later.
  • Use nmcli connection modify to change DNS for a profile and then bring it up to apply.
Pro Tip

Use nmcli in scripts for repeatable configuration and nmtui when interactively adjusting settings on a headless server.

screens.title: Creating a Persistent Static Profile with nmcli
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a persistent static profile with nmcli ensures your IP, gateway, and DNS survive reboots. The basic flow is: choose a connection name and target interface, run nmcli connection add with type ethernet, set ip4 using CIDR notation, and add gw4 for the gateway. After creation, run nmcli connection up to activate the profile. If you need the profile to use specific DNS servers, modify the profile with nmcli connection modify "ProfileName" ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4". A concrete example from the chapter: sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name "Static_enp0s8" ifname enp0s8 ip4 172.16.1.50/24 gw4 172.16.1.1 then sudo nmcli connection up "Static_enp0s8". A common misuse is forgetting to bind the profile to the correct ifname; if the interface name does not match, the profile might not apply. After activation, validate with ip addr show and ip route show. If NetworkManager manages DNS, do not overwrite /etc/resolv. conf manually; instead modify the profile so NetworkManager writes the correct entries. Creating a Persistent Static Profile with nmcli means use nmcli to make durable connection profiles and modify them for dns so settings persist and are centrally managed.. In practical terms, step through creating, modifying, and activating a static connection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Persistent Static Profile
Create and Activate
sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name "Static_enp0s8" ifname enp0s8 ip4 172.16.1.50/24 gw4 172.16.1.1
sudo nmcli connection up "Static_enp0s8"

# verify
ip addr show enp0s8
ip route show
Modify DNS
sudo nmcli connection modify "Static_enp0s8" ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4"
sudo nmcli connection up "Static_enp0s8"
Misconception

Editing /etc/resolv.conf manually may be overwritten by NetworkManager; prefer changing the connection profile.

screens.title: DNS Resolution and /etc/resolv.conf
screens.narratorSegment: DNS maps names to IP addresses and is essential when you expect to reach hosts by name. Traditionally, /etc/resolv. conf lists nameserver entries and search domains. However, many modern distributions use systemd-resolved which manages DNS and may replace or symlink /etc/resolv. conf to a dynamically generated file. When systemd-resolved is active, you might see /etc/resolv. conf point to a stub file that forwards queries to a local resolver. To change DNS reliably on such systems, modify the NetworkManager profile or edit /etc/systemd/resolved. conf if you manage resolved directly. If you manually create a static /etc/resolv. conf, you must ensure NetworkManager or resolved will not overwrite it — this is generally discouraged on managed systems. A common diagnostic: if you can ping an external IP but cannot ping by hostname, it’s almost certainly a DNS issue. Check nameservers in /etc/resolv. conf and the status of systemd-resolved with systemctl. Example: cat /etc/resolv. conf will show nameserver lines; if they are incorrect or empty, update the profile that manages DNS. Takeaway: understand which service owns resolv. conf before making changes. DNS Resolution and /etc/resolv.conf means always check whether systemd-resolved or networkmanager manages resolv.conf before editing it directly to avoid being overwritten.. In practical terms, how name resolution is configured and what systemd-resolved does. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: ping, traceroute, and ss for Diagnosis
screens.narratorSegment: Use the right tool for the symptom. Start with ping to check basic reachability and latency by sending ICMP echo requests; pinging a gateway or an external IP quickly shows whether packets are reaching the network. If ping by IP works but ping by hostname fails, it’s a DNS problem. traceroute (or tracepath) shows the path packets take and where delays or drops appear — useful when connectivity fails beyond your network. ss -tulpn lists listening sockets and their owning processes so you can verify that a service is bound to the expected port. Together these tools let you separate layers of the network stack: ping tests layer 3 reachability, traceroute identifies path issues and where hops increase latency, and ss inspects local services at layer 4. A common misconception is that a successful ping guarantees application-level success; it does not. Application issues can still occur if services are not listening or firewalls block ports. Example checks: ping -c 4 8.8.8.8; traceroute google. com; ss -tulpn | grep :80. End with a targeted test: can you reach the service port from another host?

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: Network changes are powerful and can remove your access if done carelessly. The most common mistake is misconfiguring IP, subnet, or gateway so that the host no longer has a path to management networks. Another frequent error is editing /etc/resolv. conf manually while NetworkManager or systemd-resolved controls it — your edits may be overwritten. Firewalls are often overlooked; a correctly configured IP and route can still fail because a firewall blocks traffic. When working on a remote server, always prepare a rollback: schedule a cron job that reverts the change after a few minutes or ensure out-of-band console access. For testing, use a dummy address or a secondary interface so production settings remain undisturbed. Also avoid assuming that a successful ping equals a functioning application; confirm the service with ss and by attempting an application-level connection. Finally, back up current configuration outputs before editing so you can restore them quickly. These protections reduce risk and make troubleshooting reversible. screens.title: Putting It All Together: A Troubleshooting Scenario
screens.narratorSegment: Here’s a typical troubleshooting narrative you’ll use in the field. Symptom: the server can ping external IPs like 8.8.8.8 but ping google. com fails. First, confirm routing is correct with ip route show and identify the default gateway. Second, check that the interface used by the route has an IP and is UP with ip addr show and ip link show. Third, inspect /etc/resolv. conf to see which nameservers are listed and whether the file is managed by systemd-resolved. If resolv. conf contains no usable nameserver or points to a stub but resolved is inactive, name resolution will fail. Use systemctl status systemd-resolved to verify the resolver service. If NetworkManager controls DNS, modify the profile with nmcli connection modify "Profile" ipv4. dns and bring it up. If you need to test quickly, add a temporary entry to /etc/hosts for the short term, but do not rely on hosts as a permanent solution. Finally, re-run ping by name to confirm resolution works. The key is isolating whether the problem is routing, DNS, or a local firewall. fullNarratorScript:
Networking links your Linux system to other machines, services, and the wider Internet. In this chapter you will learn the names and roles of common interfaces, how to inspect and change addresses with the ip command, and when to use NetworkManager’s nmcli and nmtui to make persistent settings. You will also inspect DNS configuration through /etc/resolv. conf and systemd-resolved, and practice basic troubleshooting with ping, traceroute, and ss. Together these skills let you diagnose why a server can reach an IP but not a hostname, how to add a temporary IP for testing, and how to create a persistent static profile with nmcli so a server keeps its address across reboots. I’ll show concrete command examples and safety checks so you won’t lock yourself out when working remotely. By the end of the lesson you’ll be able to read an interface’s state, test reachability, and take safe corrective action. Consider: what’s the first file you check when name lookups fail?

These objectives break the chapter into clear, verifiable skills you will practice. First, you will identify common network interfaces and explain their purpose, including the loopback device which lets a system communicate with itself for local testing. Second, you will use the ip command family to read addresses, bring links up or down, and inspect the routing table — skills you will use every time you check connectivity or make a temporary change. Third, you will manage NetworkManager connections with nmcli and nmtui, create a persistent static profile, and change DNS entries safely. Fourth, you will validate DNS and connectivity using ping, traceroute, and ss, and interpret outputs to distinguish a routing problem from a name resolution issue. Each objective includes a short description and a competency milestone so you know when you’re ready for hands-on work.

Each objective becomes a practical milestone you can run as commands. For interfaces, you will list interfaces with ip addr show and name the primary device used for outgoing traffic. For ip usage, you will bring an interface up and down and add a temporary address to test reachability without persisting changes. For NetworkManager, you will create a static connection profile with nmcli, set DNS servers, bring the profile up, and verify persistence after reboot. For testing, you will ping a gateway, ping by IP and by hostname to separate routing from DNS issues, and run ss -tulpn to confirm services are listening. These are concrete steps employers expect for day‑to‑day sysadmin troubleshooting, and you will practice them safely using dummy addresses or VM test interfaces. Learning Objectives — Practical Milestones means objectives map directly to commands you will run during hands-on tasks and interviews; practice them with a second interface or test vm.. In practical terms, how to prove the skill in a lab or on the job. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A network interface is the hardware or virtual device that connects your system to a network. It’s the boundary where packets enter and leave a host. Common names include lo for loopback, which is used for local-only traffic and testing; traditional eth0 or eth1 for Ethernet devices; and predictable names such as enp0s3 which tie the name to physical bus location. Knowing the name matters because commands and connection profiles target interfaces by name. For example, when adding a temporary IP you will specify the device name; when creating an nmcli profile you bind it to a specific ifname. A common misconception is that interface names are arbitrary and interchangeable — changing or misidentifying the target interface can configure the wrong device and leave your system without network. An example: if your primary interface is enp0s3 but you add a static IP to eth0, nothing will change for the active link. To confirm the active interface, use ip link show and ip addr show. Practice: run ip addr show and identify which interface has the default gateway route in the routing table. Takeaway: always confirm the interface name and link state before making changes.

The ip command family is the modern toolkit for inspecting and temporarily manipulating network state. Start by running ip addr show to list interfaces and their addresses; ip link show reveals link state and MAC addresses; ip route show prints the kernel routing table and the default gateway. These three outputs together explain where traffic will flow and whether the link is up. For example, ip route show often contains a line like default via 192.168.1.1 dev enp0s3 which tells you the gateway and the outgoing interface. When you need to test a new address without changing the persistent configuration, you can add a temporary IP with sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.100/24 dev enp0s3 and remove it with ip addr del when done. A frequent misconception is confusing temporary ip changes with persistent configuration. Remember that ip commands affect the running kernel only and will be lost after reboot. Always plan how you will persist changes if they need to survive or revert them safely if experimenting remotely. Try combining ip route get to see which interface the kernel would use toward a specific destination.

When you need to test network settings without committing them, use ip to make temporary changes. These are useful for experiments, troubleshooting, or when you need to test a new IP before persisting it. The process is: 1) identify the active interface with ip addr show, 2) bring the interface down if you must, but be careful when remote, 3) add a temporary address with ip addr add, 4) bring the link up, test connectivity, then 5) remove the address with ip addr del. Persistent configuration is handled by a network configuration service, commonly NetworkManager on many distributions. NetworkManager stores profiles and reapplies settings after reboot, so use nmcli connection add or modify to create durable profiles. A common pitfall is assuming ip changes persist — they do not. Another trap is doing link-down operations on a remote server without a safety plan. For safe remote work, schedule an automatic revert or have console access. Example: add a test IP, ping a known server, then delete the address. If it must persist, create an nmcli profile rather than editing /etc/resolv. conf directly when NetworkManager manages the file.

NetworkManager is a background service that centralizes network configuration and makes it easier to manage dynamic and persistent connections. It stores connection profiles you can list with nmcli connection show and the device state with nmcli device status. nmcli is the command-line interface that lets you create, modify, bring up, or bring down profiles. nmtui is a curses-based interactive interface useful on systems without a graphical environment. Use nmcli connection add to create a static profile: specify type ethernet, con-name, ifname, ip4 with CIDR, and gw4 for the gateway. After creating a profile, nmcli connection up will activate it. If you need to change DNS for that profile, use nmcli connection modify "Name" ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4". A misconception is that editing resolv. conf directly is always the right approach. When NetworkManager or systemd-resolved manages the file, manual edits may be overwritten. Prefer to configure DNS through NetworkManager or resolved if they are active. Use nmtui when a guided, keyboard-driven workflow is faster, and use nmcli scripts for repeatable automation. NetworkManager, nmcli and nmtui means networkmanager manages persistent profiles and should be the primary tool for durable configuration on systems where it runs.. In practical terms, high-level network management and how to interact with it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Creating a persistent static profile with nmcli ensures your IP, gateway, and DNS survive reboots. The basic flow is: choose a connection name and target interface, run nmcli connection add with type ethernet, set ip4 using CIDR notation, and add gw4 for the gateway. After creation, run nmcli connection up to activate the profile. If you need the profile to use specific DNS servers, modify the profile with nmcli connection modify "ProfileName" ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4". A concrete example from the chapter: sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name "Static_enp0s8" ifname enp0s8 ip4 172.16.1.50/24 gw4 172.16.1.1 then sudo nmcli connection up "Static_enp0s8". A common misuse is forgetting to bind the profile to the correct ifname; if the interface name does not match, the profile might not apply. After activation, validate with ip addr show and ip route show. If NetworkManager manages DNS, do not overwrite /etc/resolv. conf manually; instead modify the profile so NetworkManager writes the correct entries. Creating a Persistent Static Profile with nmcli means use nmcli to make durable connection profiles and modify them for dns so settings persist and are centrally managed.. In practical terms, step through creating, modifying, and activating a static connection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

DNS maps names to IP addresses and is essential when you expect to reach hosts by name. Traditionally, /etc/resolv. conf lists nameserver entries and search domains. However, many modern distributions use systemd-resolved which manages DNS and may replace or symlink /etc/resolv. conf to a dynamically generated file. When systemd-resolved is active, you might see /etc/resolv. conf point to a stub file that forwards queries to a local resolver. To change DNS reliably on such systems, modify the NetworkManager profile or edit /etc/systemd/resolved. conf if you manage resolved directly. If you manually create a static /etc/resolv. conf, you must ensure NetworkManager or resolved will not overwrite it — this is generally discouraged on managed systems. A common diagnostic: if you can ping an external IP but cannot ping by hostname, it’s almost certainly a DNS issue. Check nameservers in /etc/resolv. conf and the status of systemd-resolved with systemctl. Example: cat /etc/resolv. conf will show nameserver lines; if they are incorrect or empty, update the profile that manages DNS. Takeaway: understand which service owns resolv. conf before making changes. Use the right tool for the symptom. Start with ping to check basic reachability and latency by sending ICMP echo requests; pinging a gateway or an external IP quickly shows whether packets are reaching the network. If ping by IP works but ping by hostname fails, it’s a DNS problem. traceroute (or tracepath) shows the path packets take and where delays or drops appear — useful when connectivity fails beyond your network. ss -tulpn lists listening sockets and their owning processes so you can verify that a service is bound to the expected port. Together these tools let you separate layers of the network stack: ping tests layer 3 reachability, traceroute identifies path issues and where hops increase latency, and ss inspects local services at layer 4. A common misconception is that a successful ping guarantees application-level success; it does not. Application issues can still occur if services are not listening or firewalls block ports. Example checks: ping -c 4 8.8.8.8; traceroute google. com; ss -tulpn | grep :80. End with a targeted test: can you reach the service port from another host?

Follow a disciplined checklist when examining and testing network configuration. First, list interfaces and addresses with ip addr show and identify the primary interface. Then run ip link show to check link states and ip route show to find the default gateway. Next, check DNS with cat /etc/resolv. conf and determine whether systemd-resolved or NetworkManager manages it. For connectivity tests, ping your default gateway, then ping an external IP such as 8.8.8.8, and finally ping google. com to check name resolution. If name resolution fails but IP ping succeeds, adjust DNS via the manager that owns resolv. conf. Use traceroute to locate any path problems beyond your gateway. Check local services with ss -tulpn to ensure the server listens on expected ports. When experimenting with temporary addresses, add them with ip addr add, test, then remove them to leave the host as you found it. A key safety step: when working remotely, schedule a revert or ensure console access in case you lose connectivity after a change. After each step, document outputs so you can explain your conclusions. Network changes are powerful and can remove your access if done carelessly. The most common mistake is misconfiguring IP, subnet, or gateway so that the host no longer has a path to management networks. Another frequent error is editing /etc/resolv. conf manually while NetworkManager or systemd-resolved controls it — your edits may be overwritten. Firewalls are often overlooked; a correctly configured IP and route can still fail because a firewall blocks traffic. When working on a remote server, always prepare a rollback: schedule a cron job that reverts the change after a few minutes or ensure out-of-band console access. For testing, use a dummy address or a secondary interface so production settings remain undisturbed. Also avoid assuming that a successful ping equals a functioning application; confirm the service with ss and by attempting an application-level connection. Finally, back up current configuration outputs before editing so you can restore them quickly. These protections reduce risk and make troubleshooting reversible. Here’s a typical troubleshooting narrative you’ll use in the field. Symptom: the server can ping external IPs like 8.8.8.8 but ping google. com fails. First, confirm routing is correct with ip route show and identify the default gateway. Second, check that the interface used by the route has an IP and is UP with ip addr show and ip link show. Third, inspect /etc/resolv. conf to see which nameservers are listed and whether the file is managed by systemd-resolved. If resolv. conf contains no usable nameserver or points to a stub but resolved is inactive, name resolution will fail. Use systemctl status systemd-resolved to verify the resolver service. If NetworkManager controls DNS, modify the profile with nmcli connection modify "Profile" ipv4. dns and bring it up. If you need to test quickly, add a temporary entry to /etc/hosts for the short term, but do not rely on hosts as a permanent solution. Finally, re-run ping by name to confirm resolution works. The key is isolating whether the problem is routing, DNS, or a local firewall. These core concepts summarize the practical knowledge you will apply. First, interfaces are named endpoints that bind IP addresses and link state; always confirm the correct interface before making changes. Second, the ip command provides immediate control and inspection of interface addresses, link state, and routing; changes made with ip are temporary and intended for testing. Third, NetworkManager with nmcli and nmtui manages persistent connection profiles and DNS settings on systems where it runs; prefer nmcli for automation and nmtui for guided interactive edits. Fourth, DNS configuration is controlled by resolv. conf and possibly systemd-resolved; identify the owner before editing. Fifth, basic troubleshooting uses ping for reachability, traceroute for path analysis, and ss to confirm listening services. Keep in mind safety: always have a rollback plan when altering network settings remotely. Use these ideas together to diagnose and fix connectivity problems reliably.

Keep three practical reminders in mind. First, check interface names and link state with ip addr and ip link before changing network settings. Second, ip gives you fast, ephemeral control; use nmcli to make changes persistent and modify DNS for managed profiles. Third, when troubleshooting, separate routing from DNS and services: ping tests reachability, traceroute finds path problems, and ss confirms local services.
